claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy has a single-phase BCC structure.
The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy has high density.
The baseline alloy has insufficient room-temperature ductility.
Adding 2-5 at.% Al to Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr will trigger secondary-phase precipitation.
The Al-induced secondary phase will be an intermetallic B2 or Laves phase.
The secondary intermetallic phase will form a reticulated network within the BCC matrix.
The secondary-phase network will deflect and blunt cracks and prevent catastrophic crack propagation.
Coherent or semi-coherent interfaces between the secondary phase and matrix will facilitate dislocation transmission.
These interfaces will relieve stress concentrations and enhance ductility without significantly compromising strength.
The modified alloy will achieve room-temperature tensile elongation greater than 10%.
The modified alloy will maintain or slightly increase strength relative to the baseline.
Adding Al and forming the secondary phase will cause a minor increase in density.
Al is lighter than the base-alloy elements and may offset a density increase associated with the secondary phase.
The beneficial mechanism is effective specifically within approximately 2-5 at.% Al.
Excessive Al will produce brittle intermetallic phases that degrade ductility.
The identity and morphology of the secondary phase may vary with Al concentration and processing conditions.
Alloys containing 2-4 at.% Al should exhibit both a secondary intermetallic network and improved compression ductility relative to the Al-free control.
An alloy containing 6 at.% Al should exhibit degraded ductility because of excessive brittle-phase formation.

contradictions.description: The operating regime and experiment use room-temperature compression, but the quantified ductility outcome is tensile elongation greater than 10%; tensile elongation is not an outcome obtainable from the specified compression test.

The hypothesis predicts a density increase from adding Al while simultaneously attributing an offsetting effect to Al being lighter than the base elements; the net-density rationale is internally unclear and unsupported.
